A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FLOP research, with matching authors, methods and retained experiments. Text, equations, algorithms, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations measuring graph recovery, runtime and ablation effects on random graphs, paths and bnlearn network structures, including appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulations and adds nonlinear experiments, causalAssembly and Sachs evaluations, parameter sensitivity tests and a GOLEM comparison.

M1.justification: Sections 2 and 3.2 correct the specified local score from n times conditional variance to n times its logarithm, retaining the penalty. Warm-start grow-shrink, Cholesky updates, initialization and ILS remain unchanged. This is a scoring-formula correction; the PDFs do not establish a corresponding implementation change.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's simulated linear ANMs, v2 adds nonlinear MLP and Gaussian-process mechanisms, semi-synthetic manufacturing data from causalAssembly, and real protein-signaling data from Sachs (Appendices C.7–C.9). These substantially broaden the represented data and assumption-violation scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds nonlinear DAGMA to the MLP/GP comparisons in Figure 12 and unequal-noise-variance GOLEM to the standard ER comparison in Appendix C.12. These introduce substantive comparators addressing nonlinear modeling and the suitability of continuous-method assumptions. The earlier comparator sets are otherwise retained; DirectLiNGAM is not new.

E3.justification: New protocols include 25-node, degree-4 nonlinear graphs, 5000-observation causalAssembly resamples, Sachs bootstraps from 853 observations, and penalty/perturbation sweeps. Nonlinear evaluations compare SHD with distance from the exact BIC optimum. Existing core settings remain; corrections from 50 to 25 nodes in Figure 3's caption and from degree 8 to 16 in the dense-ER appendix resolve inconsistent descriptions without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: v2 adds sensitivity analyses for the BIC penalty and ILS perturbation strength (Appendix C.10, Figure 14), plus substantial score-versus-recovery diagnostics under standard and misspecified settings (Figures 5, 12 and 13). Earlier runtime, initialization and restart ablations remain; the pre-FLOP labels rename existing ablations.

E5.justification: v2 introduces explicit resampling procedures: 50 samples with replacement for causalAssembly and 50 bootstrap samples for Sachs. The original 50-instance simulation practice and Figure 2's standard-deviation bars remain. There is no reported increase in repetitions for retained experiments or new confidence-interval/significance-testing framework.

E6.justification: Substantial results are added: Figure 12 reports FLOP100 reaching the BIC optimum in 44% of MLP and 72% of GP cases, versus BOSS at 12% and 16%. Sachs results report mean SHD 12.58 for FLOP20/BOSS/GES and 11.7 for DAGMA. The retained uniform-noise comparison also revises DirectLiNGAM's plotted SHD sharply downward, from approximately 200 to near zero (v1 Figure 5; v2 Figure 7), without explaining the revision.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the Gaussian BIC expression, explicitly states faithfulness for asymptotic consistency, and adds an empirical-covariance validity qualification. Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3 and their proofs are retained, as is the Cholesky derivation moved from Appendix A to B.

C1.justification: The abstract and four principal FLOP contributions remain. Section 6 now explicitly conditions successful graph recovery on the true graph being Gaussian-BIC-optimal and emphasizes developing suitable scoring criteria. This refines the earlier conclusion that BIC optimization on standard benchmarks is largely solved.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops v1's distinction between optimization and causal recovery through nonlinear and causalAssembly failure analyses and stronger applicability qualifications. Appendix C.12 explains the mismatch between standardized data and DAGMA's assumptions and motivates the unequal-variance GOLEM comparison. The discussion more clearly attributes poor recovery to score misspecification or insufficient samples despite successful optimization.

D1.justification: v2 adds a concrete pip installation command, replacing the earlier Python/R availability wording. It documents the nonlinear generator's 100-unit sigmoid hidden layer, the GP kernel, GOLEM's gCastle version and defaults, and the software's fixed perturbation setting. Core hardware and implementation information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 credits earlier causal-search uses of ILS by Liu et al. and Nazaret and Blei, adds recent order-based work, GOLEM and equal-variance theory, and dataset references. Its principal positioning relative to BOSS and continuous optimization remains. The Benchpress preprint-to-journal update concerns the same work.

P1.justification: Most introductory and methodological prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Changes are concentrated in the rewritten discussion, a new high-level algorithm overview, numbered benchmark subsections, acknowledgments and localized clarifications. Author and conference-header text also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds BIC comparisons, an algorithm flowchart, nonlinear and causalAssembly plots, and sensitivity panels (Figures 5, 6 and 12–14). Earlier figures are retained and renumbered, with revised captions, labels and conference formatting. Some labels introduce errors: Figure 11 displays BICtrue minus BICtrue, while Figure 12's difference label has the opposite sign from the plotted optimality gaps.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the distinction central to the paper: efficient BIC optimization does not guarantee accurate causal recovery. New misspecification and real-data evaluations, more suitable continuous comparators, and sensitivity checks make that boundary assessable rather than mainly cautionary. Correcting the BIC formula and stating assumptions also improve precision. Erroneous BIC-axis labels and the unexplained DirectLiNGAM revision detract from reporting quality, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and applicability analysis.
